introduction.text: **Before you start.** `CUI-3` studied eight traditions through one lens, a few dishes each. This course goes deep into **three traditions you choose**, from `CUI-3` or new ones. In each you move from cooking dishes to cooking *from principles*: the extended pantry and its regions, two signature techniques practised to a high standard, and a regional meal designed and cooked without recipes.
Every deep dive follows the same 14-hour template, one module per tradition:

items.text: **Pantry and regions in depth** (`L1`): the extended pantry, regional variation, seasonality, history and where to buy it in the Netherlands.
**Signature technique I** (`L2`) and **II** (`L3`): the techniques that define the tradition, each practised twice.
**A regional menu** (`L4`): a three-dish meal of one region, designed and cooked without recipes, with a written rationale through the `CUI-3` lens.

introduction.text: The three modules differ in what they add. `CUI-4.M1` uses the deep-dive catalogue of the course file as its guide. `CUI-4.M2` adds a written comparison of the first two traditions. `CUI-4.M3` is planned **without the catalogue**: you write your own catalogue entry from sources before cooking, which also opens a tradition outside the catalogue.
**Respect and adaptation,** as in `CUI-3`. Each tradition is regional and alive. Adaptations to a Dutch kitchen are allowed, and named in every exercise with their effect:

items.text: Dutch seasonal vegetables stand in for produce that is out of season or flown in;

pantry goods (spices, rice, noodles, pulses, dried chillies, *masa harina*, olive oil, citrus) come from specialist shops: Turkish, Moroccan and Surinamese shops, Asian supermarkets and *tokos*, Italian and Spanish delicatessens, and online;
meat and fish are Dutch or North Sea, by the rules of the earlier courses;
nuts are replaced by seeds by default, as in S3, with the allergen rule where you use them.
forcemeats and minced fillings to the minced row (68 °C for 17 seconds, or a row of its table);
poultry to 75 °C or the poultry table, fish to 63 °C;
raw fish in *sushi* only if frozen first by the fish row, and never for risk groups;
cooked rice and stocks cooled by the cooling rule; frying by `HEA-2.M4`; allergens named for guests.

introduction.text: A probe reading below the §9 figure is a gate **Fail** in every exercise.

Plan about seven weeks at 6.5 hours a week, roughly two weeks per tradition, with the regional meal at the end of each, often with guests. You can spread the three traditions through S4 between other courses, so each is cooked in a season that suits its region.

**Have ready:** the `CUI-3` lens and your `CUI-3` notes; the course file's catalogue; the equipment of the traditions you choose (only those: the catalogue names it per tradition); the instant-read thermometer and, for frying, the frying thermometer; tasting forms, the calibrated form and tasters' cards; a budget of about €30 per extended pantry.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `CUI-4.M1` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** cooking from principles starts with knowing what the tradition cooks with, where, and when. A pantry map and a blend of your own are the base the rest of the deep dive stands on.

**You need:** the catalogue entry of your first tradition; your `CUI-3` notes on it; a notebook; a budget of about €30 for the pantry; a mortar and pestle or a spice grinder; whole spices for the blend; small jars and labels; the ingredients for one stated dish to taste the blend in.
**Explanation:**

*The extended pantry.* Beyond the core pantry of `CUI-3`, the ingredients that make regional cooking possible. For the Italian entry, that is *Carnaroli* rice, *polenta*, *guanciale*, anchovies, dried porcini. Write each on your map with three facts: what it does in the food, how it is stored, and how long it keeps.

*Regional variation.* The tradition is a set of regions with their own climate, produce, fats and dishes. Normandy cooks with butter, cream and apples; Provence with olive oil and herbs. Choose one region now for the menu of `CUI-4.M1.L4`.

*Seasonality.* Every tradition has its own calendar of what is cooked when. Map it onto the Dutch seasons, and place the deep dive in a season that suits the region: a Provençal summer menu in August, an Alsatian menu with Dutch white asparagus in spring.
*History.* Trade, migration, religion and climate shape a region's food. Trace one dish to its origins from at least two sources (the reading method of `CUI-3.M1.L2`), and write a short paragraph.

*Sourcing.* For each pantry item: where you buy it in the Netherlands, at what price and quality (Good and Best), and what you substitute when it is not found. Buy only what the menu needs, not the whole list.
*The spice blend.* The tradition's characteristic blend or seasoning (*herbes de Provence*, *ras el hanout*, a *garam masala*, *shichimi*, a *mole* spice base), composed by you for a stated dish:

items.text: write the dish and what the blend must do in it (warmth, freshness, smoke, heat);
toast the whole spices that are toasted in the tradition; grind them;
mix in parts by weight, starting from a small batch; taste it in the dish, adjust, and write the final parts and the reason for each.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Pantry and blend (60 min).** Taste the pantry items you bought, raw and cooked (a little oil in a pan, a spoon of the cooking liquid). Compose your blend for the stated dish and taste it in the dish.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a written pantry map with sources and substitutions;
a blend whose reason is written and whose taste is balanced in the dish: no single spice shouting.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A map that reads like one national cuisine
Name the region of each item and dish
The whole pantry list bought first
Write the job of each spice

blocks.text: **Safety:** allergens in the pantry named (sesame, mustard, celery, gluten in some blends and sauces; nuts replaced by seeds by default). Toast spices over moderate heat and stay with the pan.
**Record:** the pantry map, the region chosen and why, the history paragraph, and the blend with its parts and reasons.

**Why it matters:** the defining technique is what makes a tradition's food taste like itself. Practised twice, once as the tradition makes it and once with a predicted new combination, it becomes something you can cook from principles rather than from a recipe.

**You need:** the catalogue entry; two sources on the technique; the extended pantry; Dutch seasonal produce; the tradition's equipment (for example a wide heavy pan for risotto, a couscoussier, a *comal*); the thermometer; tasting forms and tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**

*The defining technique.* The catalogue names it for each tradition: a regional braise, risotto and polenta, a slow pulse stew, couscous by hand, the *tandoor* adapted for home, hand-made noodles, *sushi*, *mole*.
*The method and its cues.* Study it from at least two sources. Write the steps, then mark the critical points, the moments that decide the result, and the faults to expect. For risotto:

items.text: the rice toasted until translucent at the edges;
the hot stock added in stages, stirring;
the *mantecatura*, butter and cheese beaten in off the heat;
the wave (*all'onda*) when the pan is shaken.

blocks.text: *The high standard.* Before cooking, describe in writing what the dish looks, smells and tastes like when it is right. After cooking, check the result against it, point by point. The description is your judge, not the clock.

*Practising twice.* The first time, follow the tradition closely. The second time, cook a new combination: a Dutch seasonal ingredient (pumpkin in a risotto in autumn), a new filling or a new garnish. Write the predicted effect on taste and texture before you cook it, then let tasters judge it with the form.

*Safety.* Name the §9 row that applies to the technique in your plan: a *coq au vin* is poultry (75 °C or the poultry table); a *fabada* uses common beans (the bean row); a *tandoori* chicken goes to 75 °C.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** Cook it from the method. Check the result against your written standard and note each point met or missed.
**A new combination (90 min).** The same technique with a seasonal Dutch ingredient or a new element. Write the prediction first; tasters' cards and the form after.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the result matches the written description of the standard;
the prediction for the new combination is checked honestly, including where it was wrong.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A result short of the standard
A critical point skipped because the clock said so
Cook to the cue, not the time
A different dish, not a new combination
Change an ingredient, keep the method

blocks.text: **Safety:** the §9 row of the technique named in the plan and logged (probe readings for meat, poultry and fish). Hot stock and long-simmered sauces spit: a lid ready and long sleeves (`SAF-1`).
**Record:** the written standard; the checklist after the first cook; the prediction and the tasters' verdict for the second; photos; the probe log.

**Why it matters:** the second technique is learned as a family, so that several dishes follow from it. It is also where most of the tradition's safety rows sit: forcemeats, frying, raw fish, a reused stock.

**You need:** the catalogue entry; two sources; the pantry; the equipment of the technique (a terrine mould or loaf tin, a baking steel, a frying pot and frying thermometer, a steamer, a *tawa*); the instant-read thermometer; tasting forms and tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**

*The second technique or a preparation family,* from the catalogue: *pâtés* and *terrines*, pizza and focaccia, salt cod and *escabeche*, flatbreads, fermented batters, red-braising, *tempura*, *tamales*.

*A family, not a dish.* Learn the technique so that several dishes follow: several fillings, shapes or sauces. A forcemeat by ratio (meat, fat, salt at about 1.5–1.8 %, a panade or egg) gives a country *terrine*, a game *terrine* and a vegetable-studded one. A *tamal* dough gives a pork, a chicken and a bean filling.
*Practising twice,* as in `CUI-4.M1.L2`: once close to the tradition, once as a new combination with a written prediction.
*Safety by family.* Name the §9 row for the technique:

rows: The minced row at the core (68 °C for 17 seconds; 75 °C with poultry); cooled by the cooling rule; kept at most 2 days or frozen
Desalted in the fridge for 24–48 hours, water changed several times; *escabeche* kept cold, eaten within 2 days
The stock brought to the boil, cooled by the cooling rule and frozen between uses
Raw fish only if frozen first by the fish row (−20 °C in all parts for 24 hours, or bought so treated); never for risk groups
Meat fillings by the minced or poultry rows

blocks.text: Taste a forcemeat before it is baked by poaching a spoonful: seasoning is fixed once it sets.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** Cook it, photograph it, check it against the written standard.
**A new combination (90 min).** A second version of the family with a predicted change; tasters' cards and the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: two dishes of the family to standard;
the safety row met and logged where there is one.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The family learned as a single recipe
Write what is fixed and what varies

blocks.text: **Safety:** the row in the table above, named in the plan and logged. A *terrine* is probed in the very centre.
**Record:** the family's fixed and variable parts; the probe readings; photos of both dishes; the tasters' verdict.

**Why it matters:** a regional meal designed without recipes is the proof of cooking from principles. Recreating a dish from a description alone, with a plan and a fallback, is the judgment `JD-CHSE` level 4 asks for.

**You need:** the pantry; seasonal Dutch produce; descriptions of the dishes (from a regional cookbook's text, a menu, or a memory), but not their recipes; the day plan; the alcohol-free drinks; tasters' cards with the descriptions on them.
**Explanation:**
*Designing a regional meal without recipes:*

items.text: three dishes from one region, chosen for balance through the `CUI-3` lens: pantry, techniques, flavour profile, meal structure;
at least two of them recreated from a description alone, each with a written plan and a fallback for its riskiest step;
the seasonal Dutch substitutions named, with their effect;
the drinks the region serves with it, and an alcohol-free option for every guest (assessment §9).

blocks.text: *Balance.* Three rich braises compete. A Burgundian menu might be a vegetable *velouté*, a *bœuf bourguignon* with its garnish, and a fruit tart: light, rich, sharp.

*Recreating from a description.* Read the description; list the components it names; work out the technique for each from what you know; write the steps and the cues. Then write a fallback for the step most likely to fail: "if the sauce is thin when the meat is done, lift the meat out and reduce the sauce alone".
*The rationale.* One page through the lens: why these dishes, how they fit the region, and what was adapted.
*The day plan.* What is made the day before (a braise, which can wait; a *terrine*, which needs pressing), what on the day, and the order of service.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The regional meal (2–3 h on the day, prepared the day before).** Cook it from the plan for the household or guests. Photograph each dish. Give the tasters cards with the descriptions to hand, and ask whether they recognise each recreated dish.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the tasters recognise each recreated dish from its description;
the rationale names the pantry, the techniques, the flavour logic and every adaptation.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: One rich dish, two that contrast
A recipe found and followed later
Plan from the description only; note what you looked up
A failed step with nothing to do
Write one for the riskiest step

blocks.text: **Safety:** a braise made the day before is cooled by the cooling rule and reheated until steaming hot throughout, once (assessment §9); every protein to its row; allergens named on the cards; an alcohol-free option for every guest.
**Record:** the menu, the rationale, the plan with fallbacks, the photos, the cards, and the adaptations with their effect.

exercises.title: The two signature techniques, each practised twice
exercises.description: The two signature techniques, each practised twice.

blocks.text: **Task:** cook the first tradition's two signature techniques to a high standard, and extend each with a predicted new combination. Practise each technique twice: the second practice of each is a new combination with a written prediction, cooked and judged by tasters with the form. Compose your spice blend of `CUI-4.M1.L1` for a stated dish, with a written reason, and have the tasters judge it.
**You need:** the extended pantry; Dutch seasonal produce; meat or fish by the rules of the earlier courses; the equipment of the two techniques; the thermometer; tasters' cards and the form.
**Framework:** the catalogue entry and the technique framework.

rows: Written before cooking: look, smell, taste, texture
The §9 row of the technique, logged
As the tradition makes it, from two sources
Same technique; one ingredient or element changed; prediction written first
Composed for a stated dish, parts by weight, reason written

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Write the standard for each technique and the §9 row that applies.
Cook each technique once as the tradition makes it; photograph; compare with the standard.
Write the two new combinations with predictions; cook them; collect cards and the form.
Compose the blend for a stated dish; write the reason; collect the tasters' verdict.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`FL-ARCH` level 4:** two new combinations composed with written predictions, cooked; the cards and the form show whether the predictions held.
**`IN-ARO` level 4, the blend part:** a blend composed for a stated dish with a written reason, judged balanced by the tasters. The blind identification and the correction test were completed in S3.

blocks.text: AI review reads the standards, photos, predictions and cards: *competent* is two techniques that meet their written standards, predictions written before cooking and checked honestly, and a blend the tasters judge balanced; *not yet* is a standard written after the result, a second practice that changes the technique, or a missing probe log.
**Time:** 6 h over two weeks.

exercises.title: The regional menu
exercises.description: The regional menu, with a written rationale through the `CUI-3` lens.

blocks.text: **Task:** plan and cook a regional meal from principles, without recipes.

items.text: **The brief:** a three-dish meal of one region, with a written rationale through the `CUI-3` lens.
**The extension:** at least two of the dishes recreated from a description alone, each with a written plan and a fallback; the tasters asked whether they recognise them.
**The record:** the menu, rationale and plans; photos; the tasters' cards; the adaptations and their effect.

blocks.text: **You need:** the pantry; seasonal Dutch produce; the descriptions of the dishes; an alcohol-free drink for every guest.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Write the menu, the rationale and the plan with fallbacks.
Prepare the day before; cook and serve on the day.
Photograph each dish; collect tasters' cards with the descriptions to hand.
Note the adaptations and their effect.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`CK-CUIS` level 4, meal one of three:** a three-course meal within one tradition cooked from principles, the rationale naming the pantry, techniques and flavour logic and marking the adaptations.
**`JD-CHSE` level 4:** two dishes recreated from a description alone with a written plan and a fallback; the tasters recognise them.

blocks.text: AI review reads the rationale, plans, photos and cards: *competent* is a balanced menu of one region, a rationale through all parts of the lens, two plans with fallbacks written before the day, and both dishes recognised; *not yet* is a rationale that skips the adaptations, a missing fallback, or a recreated dish the tasters don't recognise.
**Time:** 4.5 h over two days.

items.question: What does the extended pantry add to the core pantry of `CUI-3`?

options.text: the regional ingredients that make regional dishes possible

items.why: Depth comes from the regional pantry.

items.question: Why choose one region for the menu?

options.text: a tradition is a set of regions with their own produce and dishes; one region gives the meal a logic

items.question: A pantry item for your menu can't be found in Dutch shops. What do you do?
items.answer: Find what it does in the dish (fat, acid, aroma, texture), choose a substitute that does the same, name the substitution and its effect in the exercise.

items.question: When is a deep dive best placed in the year?

options.text: in a season that suits the chosen region's produce and dishes, mapped onto the Dutch seasons
when the shops have a sale

items.question: A *terrine* of pork forcemeat is baked in a water bath. To what core temperature?

options.text: the minced row of §9: 68 °C for 17 seconds (or a row of its table); 75 °C with poultry

items.question: Your planned regional menu is a rich braise, a creamy gratin and a custard dessert. What is wrong, and how do you change it?
items.answer: Three rich dishes compete; swap one for a fresh or acidic dish of the region (a salad, a pickled vegetable, a fruit dessert) for balance.

items.question: What does "recreated from a description alone" mean?

options.text: from a description, menu or memory, with your own plan and a fallback

items.question: Which drinks does every menu with drinks include?

options.text: a non-alcoholic pairing for every guest

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `CUI-4.M2` in the course file, 1 of them a safety item. Pass mark 80 %, with the safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the second tradition is studied like the first, but now side by side with it. Comparing two pantries shows which choices are habits of one kitchen and which are principles shared by many.

**You need:** the catalogue entry of your second tradition; your pantry map from `CUI-4.M1.L1`; about €30 for the second pantry; the mortar or spice grinder; whole spices; jars and labels; the ingredients for one stated dish to taste the blend in; a sheet for the comparison table.
**Explanation:**

*The second tradition,* studied as in `CUI-4.M1.L1`: the extended pantry, regional variation, seasonality, history and sourcing, from the catalogue entry. Choose its region for `CUI-4.M2.L4`, and a season that suits it.
*Comparing with the first.* Lay the two pantries side by side, under five headings:

rows: Butter, olive oil, *ghee*, lard, sesame oil: which, and for what?
Rice, wheat, corn, pulses, potatoes: which carry the meal?
Vinegar, citrus, tamarind, yoghurt, wine: how is a dish brightened?
Which base is cooked first (*sofrito*, *mirepoix*, *tadka*, ginger and garlic)?
Dried chillies, pepper, a blend: where does warmth come from?

blocks.text: Then mark where the techniques meet (a braise, a flatbread, a fermented food) and where they part. Finally, explain one difference by climate or trade, from your sources.
*The second blend,* composed for a stated dish of this tradition, by the method of `CUI-4.M1.L1`: the job written first, parts by weight, tasted in the dish.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Pantry, blend and comparison (60 min).** Taste the second pantry, raw and cooked. Compose the blend and taste it in its dish. Fill a first comparison table of the two pantries.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a pantry map with sources, and a comparison table that explains as well as lists;
a balanced blend.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: No question asked of each heading
Answer "for what?" and "why here?" in each cell
The first tradition's fat and acid in everything
Check each choice against the new entry

blocks.text: **Safety:** allergens of the new pantry named (sesame, mustard, peanuts, soy, gluten, fish in sauces); nuts replaced by seeds by default. Dried chillies toasted with the extraction on: the fumes sting.
**Record:** the second pantry map; the blend with its parts and reasons; the first comparison table.

**Why it matters:** the second defining technique tests whether the habits of the first deep dive help or mislead. The method (standard first, critical points, two practices) carries over; the seasoning reflexes don't.

**You need:** the catalogue entry; two sources on the technique; the second pantry; Dutch seasonal produce; the technique's equipment (for example a couscoussier, or a steamer basket over a pot with the seam sealed with a cloth); the thermometer; tasting forms and tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**
*The defining technique* of the second tradition, from the catalogue, studied and practised as in `CUI-4.M1.L2`: the method, its critical points, the written standard and the §9 row that applies.

*An example: couscous by hand.* Semolina is rolled with water into grains, then steamed two or three times over a stew in a couscoussier, and fluffed with butter or oil between steamings. Its critical points are the feel of the grains after rolling (separate, not pasty), a steamer seam sealed so the steam goes through the grains, and the fluffing that keeps them apart. The standard you write might read: "light, separate grains, tender with no chalky centre, tasting of the stew's steam".
*What carries over:*

items.text: **helps:** writing the standard first; reading cues, not the clock; the probe log;

**misleads:** the first tradition's seasoning reflexes. A cook fresh from Italian food may reach for butter and cheese to finish; a Moroccan couscous wants butter or oil, *ras el hanout* and the stew's own broth. Taste against the new standard, not the old one.

blocks.text: *Practising twice:* once as the tradition makes it; once as a new combination (Dutch pumpkin, carrots and turnips in the couscous stew in autumn), with a written prediction.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** Cook it; check it against the written standard.
**A new combination (90 min).** Predict, cook, and have tasters judge it with the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the result meets the standard; the prediction is checked.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A dish that tastes of the first tradition
A new combination that is a different dish

blocks.text: **Safety:** the §9 row of the technique named and logged; a stew with chicken or lamb to its row (poultry 75 °C); steam burns: lift the lid away from you (`HEA-1`).
**Record:** the standard; the first-cook checklist; the prediction and the tasters' verdict; a line on which habits from the first deep dive helped and which misled.

**Why it matters:** the second family of the second tradition adds more dishes you can cook without a recipe. Its safety row is named in the plan before you start, because frying, fermenting and forcemeats each carry one.

**You need:** the catalogue entry; two sources; the pantry; the equipment (a *tawa* or cast-iron skillet, a baking steel, a deep heavy pot and frying thermometer, a blender for batters); the instant-read thermometer; tasters' cards and the form.
**Explanation:**
*The second technique or preparation family* of the second tradition, from the catalogue, practised as in `CUI-4.M1.L3`.
*An example: flatbreads.* One dough family, several breads:

items.text: **pita:** a hot steel makes the pocket puff;
***msemen*:** the dough laminated with butter or oil, folded into squares and cooked on a hot pan;
***manakish*:** a flat round topped with *za'atar* and oil.

blocks.text: Write what is fixed (the dough, its hydration, the rest) and what varies (the shape, the fat, the topping, the heat).

*A second example: fermented batters.* *Idli* and *dosa* from soaked, ground rice and *urad* dal, fermented overnight in a warm place, then steamed or spread thin on a hot pan. The batter is the family; the steamer and the *tawa* give two dishes from it.

*The safety row in the plan.* Frying (*tempura*, *pakora*) follows `HEA-2.M4`: the pot a third full, the frying thermometer in the oil, a lid ready, never water. A forcemeat or a meat filling is probed. Write the row before you start.
*Practising twice,* the second version a predicted new combination: *manakish* with a Dutch seasonal topping, or a *dosa* filled with Dutch potatoes and cabbage.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** To the standard; photographed.
**A new combination (90 min).** Predicted; tasters and the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:** two dishes of the family to standard; the safety row logged.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The family treated as one recipe
Write the fixed and variable parts
No probe or thermometer where §9 asks for one
Name the row in the plan; log it

blocks.text: **Safety:** the row of the family (frying by `HEA-2.M4`; fillings by the minced or poultry rows); a hot steel and a *tawa* stay hot long after use: oven gloves, and a note on the handle.
**Record:** the family's fixed and variable parts; photos of both dishes; the safety log; the tasters' verdict.

**Why it matters:** the second regional meal repeats the judgment of the first, and the written comparison turns two deep dives into understanding: why two kitchens solve the same problems differently.

**You need:** the pantry; seasonal Dutch produce; descriptions of the dishes; the day plan; alcohol-free drinks; tasters' cards with the descriptions; your notes and comparison table from both deep dives.
**Explanation:**
*The second regional meal,* designed and cooked without recipes as in `CUI-4.M1.L4`:

items.text: three dishes of one region, chosen for balance;
two recreated from a description, each with a plan and a fallback;
the substitutions named;
an alcohol-free drink for every guest.

blocks.text: Don't copy the first meal's structure: a Japanese set meal (*ichijū sansai*: soup and three dishes with rice) is built differently from a French starter, main and dessert, and a *mezze* spread differently again.
*The written comparison.* One page comparing the two traditions through the lens:

items.text: **pantry:** the fats, starches, acids and aromatics (your table from `CUI-4.M2.L1`);
**techniques:** where they meet and where they part;
**flavour profile:** what makes each taste like itself;
**meal structure and drinks:** how a meal is built and what is drunk with it;
**history and geography:** what explains the differences.

blocks.text: Use examples from your two meals. Explain; don't rank. "Italian cooking is better at pasta" says nothing; "an Italian *primo* is a course of its own, while a Punjabi meal brings bread or rice, *dal*, a vegetable and a *raita* together" says something.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The second regional meal (2–3 h, prepared the day before).** Cook it from the plan. Give the tasters cards with the descriptions to hand.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the recreated dishes recognised;
a comparison that explains the differences, not only lists them.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: One tradition treated as the standard
Describe each on its own terms
A menu shaped like the first
Build the meal as this region does

blocks.text: **Safety:** as in `CUI-4.M1.L4`: dishes made the day before cooled by the cooling rule and reheated until steaming hot throughout, once; every protein to its row; allergens on the cards; an alcohol-free option for every guest.
**Record:** the menu, rationale, plans and fallbacks; photos; cards; the comparison page.

exercises.title: The two signature techniques, each practised twice
exercises.description: The two signature techniques, each practised twice.

blocks.text: **Task:** cook the second tradition's two signature techniques to a high standard, and extend each with a predicted new combination. As in `CUI-4.M1.X1`: each technique practised twice, the second time as a new combination with a written prediction, judged by tasters with the form; the second tradition's blend composed for a stated dish with a written reason and judged balanced.
**You need:** the second pantry; Dutch seasonal produce; the equipment of the two techniques; the thermometer; tasters' cards and the form.
**Framework:** the catalogue entry and the technique framework of `CUI-4.M1.X1`.

rows: Written before cooking, for this tradition
The §9 row of each technique, logged
As the tradition makes it; then one change, predicted
For a stated dish, by weight, reasoned

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Write the standard for each technique and the §9 row that applies.
Cook each technique as the tradition makes it; compare with the standard.
Cook the two new combinations with predictions; collect cards and the form.
Compose and serve the blend; collect the tasters' verdict.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `CUI-4.M3` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the third deep dive has no catalogue. Writing the entry yourself, from sources, is what a cook does when meeting a new kitchen, and it is where the safety rows must be found, not given.

**You need:** at least two sources on the tradition (books, a regional cookbook, a reliable site), read by the method of `CUI-3.M1.L2`; one catalogue entry from the course file as a model; about €30 for the pantry; the mortar or grinder; jars and labels; the ingredients for one stated dish to taste the blend in.
**Explanation:**
*The third tradition without the catalogue.* Write the entry before cooking, with the same parts as the catalogue:

rows: Four or five, with what sets each apart
What each item does, how it is stored, how long it keeps
The method, the critical points, and the §9 row of each
How a meal of one region is built
Dutch seasonal produce for what is out of season or flown in

blocks.text: Use at least two sources, and note which source each fact comes from.

*A tradition outside* `CUI-3` is allowed here: for example Korean, Vietnamese, Ethiopian, Peruvian, Georgian, Indonesian or Surinamese. Indonesian and Surinamese cooking have deep roots in Dutch food culture, and their *tokos* and shops are the obvious place to source the pantry. Check the entry against your sources before cooking.
*Sourcing, seasonality and history,* as in `CUI-4.M1.L1`: where to buy each item, when the region cooks what, and one dish traced to its origins.
*The third blend,* composed for a stated dish (a *bumbu* paste, a *berbere*, a Korean seasoning paste, or the tradition's own), by the method of `CUI-4.M1.L1`.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The entry and the pantry (60 min).** Write the catalogue entry. Buy the pantry the menu needs and taste it. Compose the blend and taste it in its dish.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: an entry as complete as those of the catalogue, with sources and safety rows;
a balanced blend.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: An entry from a single source
A second source for each part
A technique with no safety line

blocks.text: **Safety:** a new pantry brings new allergens (peanuts in many Indonesian sauces, fish in fermented pastes, sesame, soy): name them in the entry. Fermented fish and shrimp pastes are pantry goods bought sealed and stored as the label says.
**Record:** the entry with its sources; the pantry map; the blend with its parts and reasons.

**Why it matters:** without a catalogue, the written standard comes from your sources. Choosing between sources that disagree, and saying why, is how a cook works from principles in a kitchen nobody has taught them.
**You need:** your entry and its sources; the third pantry; Dutch seasonal produce; the technique's equipment; the thermometer; tasting forms and tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**
*The defining technique* of the third tradition, from your own entry, practised as in `CUI-4.M1.L2`: the method, its critical points, the written standard, and the §9 row.

*Working without the catalogue.* Write the standard from the sources: what the dish looks, smells and tastes like when it is right. Sources will disagree: one says to fry the paste until the oil separates, another for a fixed time; one adds sugar, another doesn't. Where they disagree:

items.text: note both versions;
choose one, and write why (the region you are cooking, the older or more detailed source, what your pantry allows);
after cooking, note whether the choice worked.

blocks.text: That note is part of the standard for the next time.

*Practising twice.* Once as the tradition makes it; once as a new combination, with a written prediction. Keep the technique and change an ingredient: a Dutch seasonal vegetable in the paste-fried stew, a North Sea fish in a grilled dish.

*The high standard is still a high standard.* Working from your own entry does not lower the bar: the result is checked point by point against the description, and the tasters judge the second practice with the form.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** Cook it from the method; check it against the written standard.
**A new combination (90 min).** Predict, cook, and have tasters judge it with the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the standard written from sources and met.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The technique changed in the new combination
Keep the method; change one ingredient

blocks.text: **Safety:** the §9 row of the technique, from your entry, named in the plan and logged. Pastes fried in hot oil spit: a lid and long sleeves.
**Record:** the standard with its sources; where they disagreed, your choice and why; the checklist; the prediction and the tasters' verdict.

**Why it matters:** in your own entry, nobody hands you the safety row. This lesson finds it: every technique is matched to its row of assessment §9 before the first cook, and the family is practised twice.
**You need:** your entry; the §9 table (`04-assessment.md` §9); the pantry; the technique's equipment; the instant-read and frying thermometers if needed; tasters' cards and the form.
**Explanation:**
*The second technique or preparation family* of the third tradition, from your entry, practised as in `CUI-4.M1.L3`: the fixed and variable parts written, two dishes cooked.
*Finding the safety row.* Ask these questions of the technique, in order, and write each answer into the entry:

items.text: **Is there raw or lightly cooked fish?** The fish row: frozen first (−20 °C in all parts for 24 hours, or bought so treated), and never for risk groups. A home freezer at −18 °C does not qualify.
**Is there minced meat, a forcemeat or a filling?** The minced row: 75 °C, or 68 °C for 17 seconds.
**Poultry?** 75 °C, or the poultry table. **Whole cuts of meat or fish?** 63 °C for 15 seconds.
**Common beans?** The bean row: soaked at least 5 hours, the water poured away, boiled in fresh water at least 30 minutes, never in a slow cooker.
**Is it fried?** `HEA-2.M4`.
**Is a liquid reused** (a master stock)? Brought to the boil, cooled by the cooling rule and frozen between uses.
**Is it fermented or preserved?** The preserving rows: tested methods only.
**Is it made ahead?** The cooling rule, and kept as leftovers.

blocks.text: If no row fits, choose another technique for this deep dive: no safety figures from memory.
*Practising twice,* the second time a predicted new combination.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The technique as the tradition makes it (90 min).** To standard; photographed.
**A new combination (90 min).** Predicted; tasters and the form.

blocks.text: **Look for:** two dishes of the family to standard; the safety row logged.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The family treated as one recipe
Write the fixed and variable parts
A safety gap found while cooking
Run the eight questions before the first cook

blocks.text: **Safety:** the row the questions give, logged with each cook.
**Record:** the eight answers in the entry; the probe or thermometer log; photos of both dishes; the tasters' verdict.

**Why it matters:** the third meal is designed from an entry you wrote yourself, which makes it the fullest test of cooking from principles. The note looking back on three deep dives feeds the stage reflection of `MS-S4`.
**You need:** the pantry; seasonal Dutch produce; descriptions of the dishes; the day plan; alcohol-free drinks; tasters' cards with the descriptions; your notes from all three deep dives.
**Explanation:**
*The third regional meal,* designed and cooked without recipes as in `CUI-4.M1.L4`, from your own entry:

items.text: three dishes of one region, built as the region builds a meal;
two recreated from a description, each with a plan and a fallback;
the substitutions named, with their effect;
an alcohol-free drink for every guest.

blocks.text: *The day plan,* as before: what is made the day before, what on the day, and the order of service, written backwards from the time the guests sit down.

*Plan only from the plan.* Recipes found after the plan was written turn the meal back into recipe-following. If you must look something up, note what and why: that is honest, and it shows where the entry was thin.
*Looking back.* A short note, half a page, on what three deep dives taught about cooking from principles:

items.text: which habits travelled between all three (writing the standard first, cooking to cues, the safety questions);
what each tradition taught that the others didn't;
where you would start a fourth.

blocks.text: The note feeds the stage reflection (`JD-REFL`, `MS-S4.M1.L6`).
**Practice:**

items.text: **The third regional meal (2–3 h, prepared the day before).** Cook it from the plan. Give the tasters cards with the descriptions to hand.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the recreated dishes recognised; the rationale complete.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Plan from the descriptions; note any lookup
A failed step with nothing to do
One fallback for each recreated dish

blocks.text: **Safety:** as in `CUI-4.M1.L4`: dishes made the day before cooled by the cooling rule and reheated until steaming hot throughout, once; every protein to its row from your entry; allergens on the cards; an alcohol-free option for every guest.
**Record:** the menu, rationale, plans and fallbacks; photos; cards; the note looking back.
